stories.title: Australia’s battery boom is reshaping the grid, but few are sharing the power
stories.summary: Australia leads the world with one in three homes having rooftop solar and rapidly growing home battery installations, boosted by government subsidies and reaching over 500,000 systems installed. Only about 24% of battery owners join virtual power plants (VPPs), limiting grid coordination and shared financial benefits despite lower energy bills for participants. Challenges to wider VPP adoption include homeowners' desire for control, trust issues, and low export prices; future solutions may involve fairer tariffs and vehicle-to-grid technology for renters and apartment dwellers. For Sydney resident Ken Enderby, energy bills are a thing of the past. In fact, his power retailer owes him about A$600 (S$550) in credit. The former teacher estimates he is saving more than A$5,000 a year after installing a 10.5-kilowatt rooftop solar system and a 13.5 kilowatt-hour Tesla Powerwall battery at his suburban home. The solar panels and battery easily meet most of the electricity needs for his home and electric vehicle (EV). He has spent a total of A$2.87 to run his EV over the past 2½ years, plus A$345 in maintenance. Soon after installing his battery, Enderby joined a virtual power plant (VPP), which allows his energy retailer to automatically manage when the battery charges and discharges, including sending electricity back to the grid when prices are high. He retains the ability to override the system. In 2025, he made nearly. A$800 from exporting electricity.

stories.title: (EDITORIAL from The Korea Times on Aug. 24)
stories.summary: Korea's ambition to develop next-generation semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers is running into a basic but formidable constraint: electricity. A government assessment incorporating demand from its "three megaprojects" estimates that peak power demand could reach 158.4 to 165 gigawatts (GW) by 2040. That is roughly 27 GW higher than the projection made just four months earlier — equivalent to the capacity of about 19 large 1.4-GW nuclear reactors. The scale of the increase should be a wake-up call. Korea's current all-time peak demand is about 104 GW. Within 14 years, demand could therefore rise by more than half. The country's industrial ambitions will mean little if it cannot provide the electricity required to operate the factories, data centers and infrastructure behind them. Building semiconductor clusters and attracting AI investment without securing their power supply would amount to constructing engines without fuel. The latest estimate, presented at the fifth discussion meeting for the 12th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand, also warrants scrutiny. Demand from AI data centers, whose investment prospects remain uncertain, has been only partly reflected. The government must guard against both extremes: overestimating speculative projects and committing to unnecessary generation and grid capacity, or underestimating genuine demand and exposing industry to power shortages. The sharp revision in the forecast in such a short period underscores the need for a more dynamic forecasting system that is regularly updated as investment plans become concrete and actual electricity consumption patterns emerge.

body: The nightly parade of penguins on Phillip Island is a tourist favourite, but has recently taken on a more serious tone, AAP reports.
We started on some of the quieter penguin pathways to fine-tune the whole process and get it working as quickly as we can, so we can process as many penguins as we can each night.
We’ve now moved to the western end of the penguin parade, where the larger numbers are, and it’s working really well.
